tagline: Split room expenses fairly and settle up in a tap
summary: SplitMate is a shared expense tracker for students living together. Roommates log what they paid for — groceries, electricity, Wi-Fi — and the app works out everyone's balance and the fewest payments needed to settle up.
problem: Hostel and flat roommates constantly front money for each other, then lose track of who paid what. Chat messages and mental maths lead to awkward reminders, rounding arguments and money nobody remembers, and generic finance apps are built for individuals, not groups.

targetUsers.description: Shares a room with 2–4 people and pays for groceries or bills a few times a month.
needs: Log an expense in under 10 seconds

targetUsers.description: Usually pays the big bills (rent, electricity) and ends up chasing everyone.
needs: A fair, transparent history of every expense
Clear amounts to request from each person

features.name: Add shared expense
features.description: Log an amount, what it was for, who paid and who it is split between.

features.name: Live balances
features.description: See each roommate's net balance — to receive or to pay — updated after every change.

features.name: Settle-up suggestions
features.description: Get the shortest list of payments that clears every balance.

features.name: Record a payment
features.description: Mark a suggested payment as paid so balances update.

features.name: Manage roommates
features.description: Add people to the room and remove them once they are settled up.

features.name: Activity history
features.description: A timeline of expenses and payments with a category filter and delete.

features.name: Expense categories
features.description: Tag expenses as groceries, electricity, Wi-Fi, rent, food or other.

features.name: Unequal splits
features.description: Split by exact amounts or percentages instead of equally.

features.name: UPI payment requests
features.description: Send a payment link straight from a settle-up suggestion.

outOfScope: Real money transfers or UPI integration
Syncing one room across several phones
Multiple groups (e.g. room and trip) in one app
assumptions: One phone keeps the room's shared ledger, shown to roommates when settling up
Amounts are in Indian rupees and split equally
A room has between 2 and 8 people
Payments happen outside the app (cash or UPI) and are only recorded here
scopeNote: Real shared expenses need every roommate to see the same data, which means accounts and a backend. For the prototype, one device holds the room's ledger in AsyncStorage — the balance logic is identical, and syncing is listed as the first thing to add after the MVP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should expenses be split?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Unequal splits change the data model (a share per person) and the form.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should settling up work?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Pairwise debts are simpler to explain; simplified debts need an algorithm but mean fewer payments.
options: Pay back each person you owe

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when a roommate moves out?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Deleting a person with an open balance would make money silently disappear.
options: Block removal until they are settled up
Remove them and redistribute their balance

complexity.reasoning: Several related entities, state shared across four screens and a real algorithm (debt simplification) — a natural step up from single-list apps.

platform.reasoning: Roommates already have their phones out when paying, so a native app beats a spreadsheet. With Expo, one JavaScript codebase runs on both Android and iOS and can be tested instantly in Expo Go.

alternatives.name: Flutter
alternatives.tradeoff: Great UI performance, but you would learn Dart instead of building on JavaScript and React.

alternatives.name: Progressive Web App
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to share by link, but weaker offline storage and no native feel on iOS.

alternatives.name: Google Sheets
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero code, but formulas break easily and nobody enjoys editing a spreadsheet on a phone.

learningOpportunities: Sharing state across screens with Context and useReducer
Modelling money safely with integers instead of decimals
Writing and testing a greedy settle-up algorithm as pure functions
Deriving data with useMemo instead of storing duplicates
